summary: Extends Mobile IPv6 and IPv6 Neighbour Discovery so that movement within a local area can be handled locally. A Mobility Anchor Point reduces signalling to the home agent and correspondent nodes and can make handovers faster. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4140.

eli5.summary: Instead of telling everyone far away each time you move rooms inside a building, you just tell the front desk. The desk forwards your calls, so moving is quicker and quieter.

subtitle: Adds a local anchor router so a mobile device moving within one network does not have to update far-away peers each time.

tldr.problem: In Mobile IPv6 a mobile node must send binding updates to its home agent and every correspondent node whenever it moves, which causes delay and lost packets, especially when those peers are far away.
tldr.mechanism: A Mobility Anchor Point (MAP) in the visited network acts as a local home agent. The node registers a regional address with the MAP once, and afterwards only tells the MAP about movements within the MAP domain.
tldr.outcome: Only one binding update is needed to redirect traffic from the home agent and all correspondent nodes, and signalling stays local. RFC 5380 obsoletes RFC 4140.

today: RFC 5380 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4140, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its own appendix notes that at the time of writing there was no publicly known deployment of this specification.

sections.title: The Problem with Frequent Binding Updates
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv6 a mobile node sends binding updates (BUs) to its home agent (HA) every time it moves. The home agent cannot route traffic back to the right place until it receives the update, which costs at least half a round-trip delay, and longer if the mobile node waits for a binding acknowledgement. Authenticating updates to correspondent nodes needs approximately 1.5 round-trip times in the best case.

These exchanges disrupt active connections, and on wireless links they add messages over the air interface. HMIPv6 introduces the Mobility Anchor Point (MAP), a router that can sit at any level in a hierarchical network of routers, including the access router. It limits Mobile IPv6 signalling outside the local domain.

With a MAP, the mobile node sends binding updates to the local MAP instead of the distant home agent and correspondent nodes, and only one update is needed to reroute traffic from the home agent and all correspondent nodes, regardless of how many it talks to. The RFC describes a MAP as essentially a local home agent. HMIPv6 does not require a permanent home agent.
sections.eli5: When you move, telling far-away people takes a long time. A helper close by can take the message for you, so only the helper needs to know each little move.

sections.title: Overview and Terminology
sections.content:
The scheme adds one function, the MAP, and minor extensions to the mobile node. Correspondent node and home agent operation is unaffected. Like Mobile IPv6 it is independent of the underlying access technology.

The mobile node ends up with two addresses. The Regional Care-of Address (RCoA) is allocated by the MAP and lives on the MAP's subnet. The On-Link Care-of Address (LCoA) is configured from the prefix advertised by the node's default router, the access router (AR). A local binding update binds the RCoA to the LCoA at the MAP.

The MAP receives packets for the mobile node, then encapsulates and forwards them to its current LCoA. If the node changes its LCoA inside the MAP domain, it only registers the new LCoA with the MAP. The RCoA stays the same, so the movement is transparent to correspondent nodes. A MAP domain is bounded by the access routers that advertise the MAP.
sections.eli5: You have a home address that stays put at the front desk (the regional address) and a room number that changes (the local address). Mail goes to the front desk, which carries it to your current room.

sections.title: The Local Binding Update and MAP Option
sections.content:
HMIPv6 makes two small protocol additions. First, a new M flag in the Mobile IPv6 binding update indicates a MAP registration. When registering with a MAP, both the M and A flags MUST be set to tell it apart from an update sent to a home agent or correspondent node.

Second, a new IPv6 Neighbour Discovery option, the MAP option, is carried in Router Advertisements. Its Type is 23 and its Length MUST be 3. Dist is a 4-bit distance in hops from the receiver to the MAP, starting from 1 for a MAP on the same link, and zero MUST NOT be used. Pref is a 4-bit operator preference where 15 is highest, used as a tie-breaker for equal Dist. The R flag says the RCoA is allocated by the MAP using Section 9 of RFC 4877. Valid Lifetime gives the validity in seconds of the MAP address and RCoA, and the option ends with one of the MAP's global addresses.
sections.eli5: The front desk puts up a notice in the hallway (the MAP option) saying where it is, how far away, and how long the notice is good for. A small flag in your message tells the desk the note is for it.

sections.title: How Mobile Node, MAP and Peers Behave
sections.content:
When a node enters a new MAP domain it acquires an RCoA using the RFC 4877 mechanisms and sends a local BU to the MAP with the A and M flags set. The RCoA goes in the Home Address option and the LCoA is the source address. The MAP, acting as a home agent, returns a binding acknowledgement and stores the binding in its cache. A bi-directional tunnel then carries traffic: the outer header holds the LCoA and the MAP address, and the inner header the RCoA and the peer's address.

After the MAP acknowledges, the node SHOULD register the RCoA with its home agent and may send a similar update to correspondent nodes. Those lifetimes MUST NOT be larger than the lifetime granted by the MAP. The MAP intercepts packets for the RCoA using proxy Neighbour Advertisement and tunnels them to the LCoA. It has no knowledge of the home address. It may be configured with valid on-link prefixes and reject others with error code 129 (administratively prohibited).

The home agent and correspondent nodes need no changes. A node can also use its RCoA as a plain source address, so it looks like a fixed node while it moves within a MAP domain, which gives near-optimal routing but no global mobility. Because peers see only the RCoA, address-based location tracking is also harder.
sections.eli5: You tell the front desk your current room once, and the desk wraps each letter in a new envelope addressed to that room. Friends far away keep writing to the front desk and never notice you moved.

sections.title: Discovering and Choosing a MAP
sections.content:
The specification requires administrators to configure the MAP option information in access routers by hand. Dynamic MAP discovery that existed in RFC 4140 was removed. A mobile node scans the MAP options in each Router Advertisement and SHOULD register with the MAP having the highest preference. A MAP with preference zero SHOULD NOT be used for new local BUs, though existing bindings may be refreshed.

The mobile node should be eager to create new bindings and lazy in releasing old ones, which helps recover from a MAP failure. It MUST NOT use an RCoA from one MAP as the care-of address in a binding with another, because that would force repeated encapsulation, and the RFC prohibits forcing packets down a hierarchy of MAPs.

As a default algorithm, the node orders MAPs from the largest Dist and picks the first whose preference and valid lifetime are nonzero. This favours the furthest MAP to reduce re-registrations, which matters for fast-moving nodes. To speed a handover between MAPs, the node SHOULD send a local BU to its previous MAP with its new LCoA so in-flight packets are forwarded.
sections.eli5: Hallway notices tell you which front desks are nearby and how good each is. By default you pick the farthest good desk, so you do not have to change desks every time you step a few rooms over.

sections.title: MAP Failure and Tunnelling Overhead
sections.content:
A MAP, like a home agent, is a single point of failure: if it fails, its binding cache is lost. MAP redundancy is outside the scope of the RFC. A node detects failure when it sees a Router Advertisement with a MAP option whose lifetime is zero. It must then choose another MAP and create new bindings, and if none exists it MUST NOT use HMIPv6. As one example, an access router could probe the MAP every 10 seconds, then every 5 seconds for 15 seconds, before advertising a zero lifetime.

Because traffic is tunnelled between node and MAP, and may be tunnelled again if there is a home agent elsewhere, mobile nodes MUST account for the encapsulation when calculating the MTU available to upper layers.
sections.eli5: If the front desk closes suddenly, the hallway notice says so and you must find another desk. Wrapping letters in extra envelopes also makes them a bit bigger, so you have to remember that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The relationship between mobile node and MAP must be strong: it MUST involve mutual authentication, integrity protection and protection against replay attacks. Without them, malicious nodes could impersonate other nodes or a MAP and disrupt traffic from every correspondent node that knows the RCoA. Confidentiality for binding updates to the MAP is not required.

IKEv2 MUST be supported by the node and the MAP. Authorisation may be based on identity or on a certificate authority the MAP trusts, and EAP over IKEv2 MAY be used. Binding updates between the MAP and node MUST be protected with AH or ESP in transport mode, and a non-null authentication algorithm MUST be used with ESP. A return routability test is not needed for the MAP. The security relationships with correspondent nodes and the home agent are not changed by this specification.
sections.eli5: The front desk and you must prove who you are to each other and make sure nobody can tamper with your messages, or a stranger could grab your mail.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: IPv6 Neighbour Discovery option type, value 23.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the option; MUST be 3.

fields.name: Dist
fields.desc: Hops between MAP and receiver; starts at 1; zero MUST NOT be used.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Set when the MAP allocates the RCoA per RFC 4877 Section 9.

fields.name: Valid Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds the MAP address and RCoA are valid.

fields.name: Global IP Address for MAP
fields.desc: One of the MAP's global addresses.

messages.label: Local BU (A and M flags)
messages.note: Binds the RCoA to the LCoA.
